content: Sever's disease, also known as calcaneal apophysitis, is the most common cause of heel pain in children aged 8 to 13. This condition arises due to inflammation of the growth plates in the calcaneus (heel bone) at the back of the foot. It is caused by the rapid growth of the bone compared to the calcaneal tendon, also referred to as the Achilles tendon. The disease is named after J.W. Sever, who first described it in 1912. Sever's disease is directly linked to overuse of the heel bone and its associated tendons. Activities that involve repetitive heel movements, such as playing football, basketball, or lacrosse, can trigger the condition. It is often associated with starting a new sport or the beginning of a new sports season. Excessive weight-bearing on the heel or excessive traction on the developing bones and tendons can also contribute to the condition. The prognosis for Sever's disease is favorable, as it is self-limiting. The condition typically resolves on its own when the affected area is rested or when the bone completes its growth. It is not expected to cause any long-term disability and usually subsides within 2 to 8 weeks. However, the condition can recur, particularly at the start of a new sports season, if proper care is not taken. The clinical history and symptoms of Sever's disease include: Complaints of pain or tenderness in one or both heels. Discomfort upon waking or when the heel is squeezed. Limping. Increased pain after walking and difficulty walking. Pain during running or playing sports. Treatment for Sever's disease may involve one or more of the following approaches: Ceasing sports or other activities that exacerbate the condition.
